title: How Janitorial Markup & Overhead Work: Breaking Down a Commercial Cleaning Quote
seoTitle: Janitorial Company Profit Margin & Overhead: Cleaning Quote Math (2026)
metaDescription: Janitorial company profit margin overhead explained: see how $35–$65/hr US rates split W-2 payroll, taxes, COI, supplies & 10%–20% margin. Compare quotes.
excerpt: See exactly how US commercial cleaning vendors build $35 to $65 per hour labor rates and $0.05 to $0.20 per sq ft monthly retainers from frontline wages, payroll taxes, insurance, supplies, and profit margin. Use this quote audit math to spot sustainable W-2 bids versus risky 1099 underbids.
quickAnswer: Healthy US commercial cleaning companies earn a 10% to 20% net pre-tax profit margin—not the 55% to 110% gross labor markup required to convert an $18 to $24/hr cleaner wage into a $35 to $65/hr standard billed rate ($55 to $95/hr for specialty work). Across a typical $0.05 to $0.20/sq ft janitorial invoice, 52% to 68% covers loaded W-2 wages, payroll taxes, and Workers' Compensation, 8% to 14% funds chemicals, equipment, and consumables, and 10% to 18% pays for COI insurance, field supervision, and administration.

blocks.text: When an office manager reviews a janitorial proposal billing **$48 per labor hour**—or **$1,050 per visit** for a mid-size suite—it is easy to assume the cleaning contractor pockets half the check while paying frontline cleaners **$19 to $22 per hour**. In reality, commercial janitorial contracting is a high-volume, labor-intensive service business where statutory payroll burden, Workers' Compensation, liability insurance, and field supervision absorb the vast majority of that spread.

Understanding **janitorial company profit margin overhead** equips you to negotiate smarter contracts. Instead of squeezing hourly rates down to unsustainable levels that trigger skipped nights and constant crew turnover, you can audit each line of the quote against [national office cleaning cost benchmarks](/office-cleaning-cost-guides/) and isolate genuine waste from mandatory compliance costs.
Anatomy of a $35–$65/Hr Commercial Cleaning Rate (Markup vs. Profit Margin)

The single biggest misconception in facility procurement is confusing **labor markup** with **net profit margin**. Markup measures the percentage added on top of direct hourly wages to cover every direct and indirect operating cost; net profit margin is what remains after paying payroll taxes, insurance, supplies, vehicles, and branch management.

For example, if a regional contractor pays a night cleaner **$20.00 per hour** and bills the client **$45.00 per hour** (a **125% markup on base wage**), statutory payroll burden (**$4.80/hr**), job supplies and equipment wear (**$4.50/hr**), and overhead/COI/supervision (**$8.95/hr**) consume **$38.25 per hour** before profit. The contractor nets **$6.75 per hour—a 15.0% operating profit margin**.

Worked Example: Reverse-Engineering a 10,000 Sq Ft Office Cleaning Quote

To see how overhead scales onto a real monthly retainer, examine a **10,000 sq ft carpeted office** (`1.00x` flooring) with **four restrooms** serviced **3 times per week** (**13.0 visits per month** using **4.333 weeks per month** math, at a `0.95x` frequency multiplier). Inside the national `10,000–24,999 sq ft` bracket (**$0.07 to $0.12 per sq ft**) plus **$15 to $30 per restroom**, the base monthly invoice lands between **$9,425 and $16,380 per month** (**$725 to $1,260 per visit**).

Using ISSA open-office production averages of **3,500 sq ft per labor hour** plus restroom fixture detailing, a multi-person crew logs **3.10 to 4.57 direct cleaning hours** per visit inside the suite—and the vendor must also fund non-billable travel time, supply closet staging, supervisor QA audits, and optional add-ons (**$12 to $25/visit** breakroom sanitation, **$15 to $35/visit** interior glass, and **$0.012 to $0.025/sq ft/visit** consumables).

blocks.text: How Payroll Burden, Workers' Comp, and 1099 Misclassification Skew Bids

Whenever one bidder comes in **30% to 40% below** competing W-2 proposals, the discount almost never comes from superior cleaning robots—it comes from cutting out mandatory payroll taxes and insurance. Watch for these four structural distortions during quote reviews:

items: **Illegal 1099 Subcontractor Classification:** Treating nightly cleaners who follow fixed schedules and wear company uniforms as 1099 contractors shaves 15% to 22% off payroll costs by skipping FICA matching, unemployment insurance, and Workers' Compensation—exposing your company to premises-injury lawsuits and wage-and-hour audits.

**Workers' Compensation Class-Code Evasion:** Janitorial Workers' Comp premiums vary sharply by state experience modifier; underreporting payroll hours artificially lowers a bid until an audit cancels the vendor's policy mid-contract.

**Implied Hourly Rate Below $30/Hr:** Divide the monthly price (minus consumables) by visits per month and realistic crew hours (compare [hourly vs. per-visit benchmarks](/office-cleaning-cost-guides/cost-per-hour-vs-cost-per-visit-benchmarks/)). Any bid yielding under **$30 implied dollars per hour** forces cleaners to rush a 3-hour scope in 90 minutes.

**Missing 4.333-Week Averaging:** Some low-ball bids quote only 4.0 weeks per month (12 visits on a 3x/wk schedule) instead of **13.0 visits**, then tack on fifth-week surcharges or skip service four months out of the year.

blocks.title: Red Flag: Any Bid Priced Below $30 Implied Dollars Per Labor Hour
blocks.text: Because loaded US W-2 labor, payroll taxes, Workers' Comp, chemicals, and basic liability insurance cost $26 to $32 per hour before a contractor earns a single dollar of profit, bids implying under $30/hr guarantee unpaid corner-cutting, unbadged subcontractors, or zero Workers' Compensation.
Equipment Productivity, Day Porter Tools, and Consumables Margin Drivers

Legitimate contractors protect their **10% to 20% net profit margin** without raising your bill by equipping crews with ergonomic, fast-turnaround tools that trim wasted minutes per visit. On exterior entry aprons and landscaped office walkways, day porters clear windblown debris in minutes without stooping by carrying an **Unger Nifty Nabber 36-Inch Commercial Trash Picker Grabber** built with a 36-in reach, rubber-tipped steel claws, an ergonomic grip, and a 10 lb lift rating.

Inside active reception lobbies, daytime spills must be cleared discreetly without interrupting client meetings. Porters pair quiet sweeping with the **Rubbermaid Commercial Lobby Pro Upright Dust Pan & Broom**, which uses a long handle, an auto-closing debris lid, and quiet wheels engineered for day-porter shifts. For rapid executive-suite or boardroom touchups between meetings without dragging corded uprights across hallways, facilities stock the **Dyson V15 Detect Pro / Commercial Spot Cordless Stick**, featuring sealed HEPA filtration, laser dust detection, up to a 60 min run time, and a nimble 6.8 lb frame.

Consumables represent another quiet margin lever. When vendors bundle toilet tissue, roll towels, hand soap, and can liners at **$0.012 to $0.025 per sq ft per visit**, they typically mark up wholesale paper cases by **15% to 25%** to cover inventory delivery and closet stocking labor. High-headcount offices can often save 10% to 15% on supply spend by buying bulk paper directly while paying the cleaner strictly for labor to restock dispensers.
Insurance, OSHA Compliance, and Supervision Overhead You Should Want to Pay For

Cutting vendor overhead too aggressively strips away the exact safeguards that protect a commercial tenant from regulatory fines and property losses. Before signing any multi-year service agreement (see our [RFP contract comparison guide](/comparing-quotes-and-contracts/)), verify that your bidder's overhead budget explicitly funds these compliance standards.

blocks.title: Mandatory Insurance & OSHA Items Inside Legitimate Janitorial Overhead
blocks.text: Every vetted commercial contractor should budget inside overhead for: (1) an active Certificate of Insurance with $1,000,000 per occurrence / $2,000,000 aggregate General Liability naming your firm and landlord as Additional Insured, (2) statutory W-2 Workers' Compensation, (3) a janitorial fidelity bond, (4) OSHA Hazard Communication (29 CFR 1910.1200) SDS binders and secondary labels, (5) OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens (29 CFR 1910.1030) restroom training, and (6) Green Seal GS-37 / EPA Safer Choice dilution compliance.
5-Step Audit to Reverse-Engineer Any Janitorial Quote

Use this five-step audit whenever you compare two or three bids that vary by more than 20%. Plug your suite specs into our [Quote Comparator](/compare-cleaning-quotes/) to normalize add-ons automatically.

items.name: Normalize Monthly Totals by 4.333 Weeks
items.text: Divide the monthly quote by 4.33 (1x/wk), 8.66 (2x/wk), 13.0 (3x/wk), or 21.65 (5x/wk) to expose the exact per-visit price and confirm fifth-week visits are included.

items.name: Strip Out Non-Labor Add-Ons and Consumables
items.text: Subtract breakroom sanitation ($12–$25/visit), interior glass ($15–$35/visit), paper/soap consumables ($0.012–$0.025/sq ft/visit), and amortized deep floor care ($0.03–$0.06/sq ft/month) to isolate pure cleaning revenue.

items.name: Verify Implied Hourly Rate Against $35–$65/Hr
items.text: Ask each bidder how many total crew labor hours per visit are budgeted in writing, then divide isolated per-visit labor price by committed hours to verify the vendor clears $35–$65/hr.

items.name: Confirm W-2 Payroll and Full COI Endorsements
items.text: Request a sample Workers' Compensation policy page and Additional Insured COI endorsement directly from the vendor's insurance broker—never accept a verbal assurance.

items.name: Optimize Frequency Before Squeezing Margin
items.text: If a compliant W-2 quote exceeds budget, shift from 5x/week (0.90x) to 3x/week (0.95x) or supply your own bulk paper goods rather than forcing an unsafe cut in cleaner hours or hourly pay.

faqs.q: What is the average profit margin for a US commercial cleaning company?
faqs.a: Well-run US commercial janitorial companies typically earn a 10% to 20% net pre-tax profit margin on recurring office contracts. While their labor markup on direct hourly wages often looks like 60% to 110% (turning an $18 to $22/hr wage into a $35 to $65/hr billed rate), payroll taxes, Workers' Compensation, COI insurance, chemicals, and field supervision absorb most of that spread.

faqs.q: Why is a $25/hr commercial cleaning quote a major red flag?
faqs.a: Once a contractor pays a competitive US cleaning wage plus 22% to 30% in W-2 payroll taxes, Workers' Compensation, and paid sick leave, direct loaded labor alone reaches $22 to $28 per hour before buying supplies or insurance. A $25/hr bid usually indicates illegal 1099 subcontractor misclassification, missing Workers' Comp, or skipped scope tasks.

faqs.q: How does 4.333 weeks per month billing affect contractor margin and client pricing?
faqs.a: Because a 52-week year equals 4.333 weeks per month, a 3x/week schedule delivers 13.0 visits per month and a 5x/week schedule delivers 21.65 visits. Averaging over 4.333 weeks ensures the contractor receives steady revenue during five-week months without charging surprise surcharges, while clients avoid paying for four extra unworked visits in shorter months.

faqs.q: Does vendor overhead automatically include OSHA compliance and Green Seal chemicals?
faqs.a: Reputable full-service contractors include OSHA Hazard Communication (29 CFR 1910.1200) SDS compliance, OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens (29 CFR 1910.1030) training, and Green Seal GS-37 or EPA Safer Choice concentrated chemicals inside their standard overhead, adding roughly 0% to 4% over commodity cleaners. Always write these exact standards plus $1M/$2M General Liability Additional Insured COI limits into your RFP.

faqs.q: Which services sit outside base overhead and bill at specialty margins?
faqs.a: Routine per-square-foot contracts exclude quarterly or annual deep floor restoration (carpet hot-water extraction and VCT strip-and-wax at $0.03 to $0.06/sq ft/month amortized), exterior high windows, inside-refrigerator purges, paper/soap consumables ($0.012 to $0.025/sq ft/visit if bundled), and specialty restoration or biohazard cleanup billed at $55 to $95 per hour.
